sections.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
objectives: Define the first law of thermodynamics.
Describe how conservation of energy relates to the first law of thermodynamics.
Identify instances of the first law of thermodynamics working in everyday situations, including biological metabolism.
Calculate changes in the internal energy of a system, after accounting for heat transfer and work done.

misconceptions.claim: Heat added to a gas always raises its temperature.
misconceptions.correction: It can raise the temperature, do work as it expands, or both. The first law says where it goes.

summary: The first law of thermodynamics is given as ΔEint=Q−W, where ΔEint is the change in internal energy of a system, Q is the net heat transfer (the sum of all heat transfer into and out of the system), and W is the net work done (the sum of all work done on or by the system).
Both Q and W are energy in transit; only ΔEint represents an independent quantity capable of being stored.
The internal energy Eint of a system depends only on the state of the system and not how it reached that state.

authored_exercises.stem: A gas absorbs 200 J of heat and does 50 J of work. Find the change in its internal energy.
solution: Use the first law: ΔE_int = Q − W.
Q = 200 J and W = 50 J.

sections.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics and Some Simple Processes
objectives: Describe the processes of a simple heat engine.
Explain the differences among the simple thermodynamic processes—isobaric, isochoric, isothermal, and adiabatic.
Calculate total work done in a cyclical thermodynamic process.

misconceptions.claim: An isothermal process has no heat transfer.
misconceptions.correction: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, the internal energy does not change, so Q = W. Heat can enter or leave while the gas does or has work done on it.
misconceptions.signal: Isothermal means constant temperature, not zero heat.

misconceptions.claim: The temperature cannot change in an adiabatic process.
misconceptions.correction: Adiabatic means no heat transfer, not constant temperature. Work done by or on the gas changes its internal energy and therefore its temperature.
misconceptions.signal: A bicycle pump warms up because the compression is nearly adiabatic.

summary: One of the important implications of the first law of thermodynamics is that machines can be harnessed to do work that humans previously did by hand or by external energy supplies such as running water or the heat of the Sun. A machine that uses heat transfer to do work is known as a heat engine.
There are several simple processes, used by heat engines, that flow from the first law of thermodynamics. Among them are the isobaric, isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes.
These processes differ from one another based on how they affect pressure, volume, temperature, and heat transfer.

sections.title: Introduction to the Second Law of Thermodynamics: Heat Engines and Their Efficiency
objectives: State the expressions of the second law of thermodynamics.
Calculate the efficiency and carbon dioxide emission of a coal-fired electricity plant, using second law characteristics.
Describe and define the Otto cycle.

misconceptions.claim: Heat always flows from a hot body to a cold one.
misconceptions.correction: It flows that way on its own, but a refrigerator moves it the other way by doing work on it.

summary: The two expressions of the second law of thermodynamics are: (i) Heat transfer occurs spontaneously from higher- to lower-temperature bodies but never spontaneously in the reverse direction; and (ii) It is impossible in any system for heat transfer from a reservoir to completely convert to work in a cyclical process in which the system returns to its initial state.
Irreversible processes depend on path and do not return to their original state. Cyclical processes are processes that return to their original state at the end of every cycle.

In a cyclical process, such as a heat engine, the net work done by the system equals the net heat transfer into the system, or W = Q h – Q c , where Q h is the heat transfer from the hot object (hot reservoir), and Q c is the heat transfer into the cold object (cold reservoir).

authored_exercises.stem: A heat engine absorbs 500 J from a hot reservoir and does 150 J of useful work. Find its efficiency.
solution: Efficiency is useful work divided by heat absorbed.
As a percentage, e = 30%.

sections.title: Carnot’s Perfect Heat Engine: The Second Law of Thermodynamics Restated
objectives: Identify a Carnot cycle.
Calculate maximum theoretical efficiency of a nuclear reactor.
Explain how dissipative processes affect the ideal Carnot engine.

misconceptions.claim: A Carnot engine can be made 100% efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Its efficiency is 1 − T_c/T_h. That reaches 100% only if the cold reservoir is at absolute zero, which is unattainable.
misconceptions.signal: Real engines are always less efficient than the Carnot limit.

misconceptions.claim: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on the working substance.
misconceptions.correction: The maximum efficiency depends only on the absolute temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, not on the substance.
misconceptions.signal: That universality is what makes the Carnot result so powerful.

summary: The Carnot cycle is a theoretical cycle that is the most efficient cyclical process possible. Any engine using the Carnot cycle, which uses only reversible processes (adiabatic and isothermal), is known as a Carnot engine.
Any engine that uses the Carnot cycle enjoys the maximum theoretical efficiency.

While Carnot engines are ideal engines, in reality, no engine achieves Carnot’s theoretical maximum efficiency, since dissipative processes, such as friction, play a role. Carnot cycles without heat loss may be possible at absolute zero, but this has never been seen in nature.

sections.title: Applications of Thermodynamics: Heat Pumps and Refrigerators
objectives: Describe the use of heat engines in heat pumps and refrigerators.
Demonstrate how a heat pump works to warm an interior space.
Explain the differences between heat pumps and refrigerators.
Calculate a heat pump’s coefficient of performance.

misconceptions.correction: It does not create energy. It uses work to move heat from a colder place to a hotter place, delivering more heat than the work input.
misconceptions.signal: The first law is still obeyed: Q_h = Q_c + W.

misconceptions.claim: A refrigerator and a heat pump are unrelated machines.
misconceptions.correction: They use the same cycle. A refrigerator’s purpose is to remove heat from the cold space; a heat pump’s purpose is to deliver heat to the hot space. Their coefficients of performance are defined differently.
misconceptions.signal: The same device can be described either way.

summary: An artifact of the second law of thermodynamics is the ability to heat an interior space using a heat pump. Heat pumps compress cold ambient air and, in so doing, heat it to room temperature without violation of conservation principles.
To calculate the heat pump’s coefficient of performance, use the equation COPhp=QhW.
A refrigerator is a heat pump; it takes warm ambient air and expands it to chill it.

sections.title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics: Disorder and the Unavailability of Energy
objectives: Define entropy and calculate the increase of entropy in a system with reversible and irreversible processes.
Explain the expected fate of the universe in entropic terms.
Calculate the increasing disorder of a system.

misconceptions.claim: Entropy always increases in every process.
misconceptions.correction: The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. A reversible process has zero total entropy change, and a system’s entropy can fall if work is done on it and heat is removed.
misconceptions.signal: The second law is about the total, not every part.

misconceptions.claim: Entropy is just another name for heat.
misconceptions.correction: Entropy measures how spread out the energy is at a given temperature. Heat is energy in transit.
misconceptions.signal: They have different units: entropy is J/K.

summary: Entropy is the loss of energy available to do work.
Another form of the second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of a system either increases or remains constant; it never decreases.
Entropy is zero in a reversible process; it increases in an irreversible process.

authored_exercises.stem: What happens to the total entropy of the universe in a reversible process?
solution: A reversible process has no net increase in entropy.
The entropy change of the system and surroundings cancel.
The total entropy change is zero.

sections.no_exam_link_reason: Entropy is not named in either syllabus.

sections.title: Statistical Interpretation of Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics: The Underlying Explanation
objectives: Identify probabilities in entropy.
Analyze statistical probabilities in entropic systems.

misconceptions.claim: The second law forbids any system from becoming more ordered.
misconceptions.correction: Small systems can become more ordered by chance or by work done on them. The second law says the total entropy of an isolated system tends to increase; it is statistical, not an absolute ban on local order.
misconceptions.signal: Life creates local order by using energy from its surroundings.

summary: Disorder is far more likely than order, which can be seen statistically.

The entropy of a system in a given state (a macrostate) can be written as S=klnW, where k=1.38×10–23J/K is Boltzmann’s constant, and lnW is the natural logarithm of the number of microstates W corresponding to the given macrostate.
sections.no_exam_link_reason: The statistical interpretation of entropy is not named in either syllabus.

sec-8:exr-38.stem: If you toss 100 fair coins each second, verify that you can expect to get 100 heads or 100 tails once in about $2\times10^{22}$ years. Calculate the time to two-digit accuracy.
solution: The probability of 100 heads is $(1/2)^{100}$, and the probability of 100 tails is the same. The probability of either outcome is $2/2^{100}=1/2^{99}$.
At one toss per second, the expected wait is $2^{99}\ \mathrm{s}=6.34\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{s}$.
Convert to years: $(6.34\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{s})/(3.16\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s/y})=2.0\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{y}$.

sec-8:exr-43.stem: (a) If tossing 100 coins, how many ways (microstates) are there to get the three most likely macrostates of 49 heads and 51 tails, 50 heads and 50 tails, and 51 heads and 49 tails? (b) What percent of the total possibilities is this?
solution: (a) The number of ways is $\binom{100}{49}+\binom{100}{50}+\binom{100}{51}\approx9.9\times10^{28}+1.01\times10^{29}+9.9\times10^{28}=3.0\times10^{29}$.
(b) The total number of outcomes is $2^{100}=1.27\times10^{30}$, so the percentage is $(3.0\times10^{29})/(1.27\times10^{30})=24\%$.

sec-8:exr-55.stem: (a) Construct a table showing the macrostates and all of the individual microstates for tossing 6 coins. (b) How many macrostates are there? (c) What is the total number of microstates? (d) What percent chance is there of tossing 5 heads and 1 tail? (e) How much more likely are you to toss 3 heads and 3 tails than 5 heads and 1 tail? (Take the ratio of the number of microstates to find out.)
solution: (a) The macrostates are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 heads. Their microstate counts are 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1.
(b) There are 7 macrostates.
(c) The total is $2^{6}=64$ microstates.
(d) 5 heads and 1 tail has 6 microstates, so the probability is $6/64=9.38\%$.
(e) 3 heads and 3 tails has 20 microstates, while 5 heads and 1 tail has 6, so it is $20/6=3.33$ times more likely.
